newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand urged to build bond market after baht float.
newsitem.headline: Thailand urged to build bond market after baht float.

text.p: Thailand must seize the opportunity to develop its government bond market while foreign money pours into the economy after the baht's managed float, analysts and officials say.
But legal and structural hurdles must be overcome to allow the country to issue long-term benchmarks which would attract overseas investors, they said.

"We need a well-developed long-term debt-market to absorb the funds and keep them here longer...so that when foreign investors don't love us any more, the money won't flow out too fast," said Commerce Minister Narongchai Akarasanee.
"If we had a good debt market when foreign portfolio investments flooded the market in 1994-1995, we might have suffered less today," said Narongchai, a former president of a major Thai brokerage.
Prices are more volatile in shares than in debt instruments and share investors tend to withdraw their funds more quickly when sentiment turns sour, as was the case in Thailand last year.
Although state enterprises and the central bank currently issue bonds, the issues have done little to help establish a benchmark or standards for the debt market.

The longest maturity for central bank paper is two years, while state enterprise bonds are mainly of five years duration. Most of the paper is used by financial firms for for reserve obligations, and is not actively traded.
Analysts say the government has considered issuing long-term domestic bonds for some time now but current law prohibits the government from issuing bonds unless it runs a fiscal deficit.
Passing laws is a major challenge for Thailand given frequent changes in governments.
Thailand is expecting its first fiscal deficit for ten years in 1996/7 -- a 63.2 billion baht shortfall -- but so far no-one is speculating on an imminent bond issue.

Foreign investment flooded into Thailand during the past decade as its Gross Domestic Product (GDP) roared ahead at an annual rate of nine percent a year. The fast pace of growth forced the country to import capital to finance its swollen current account deficit, which stood at around 7.9 percent of GDP in 1996.
The shortfall in long-term capital financing for the current account spurred the growth rate for Thailand's external debt to an annualized average of 22 percent over the past six years.
With a total debt to GDP ratio of 42.7 percent -- excluding the bank sector -- and a debt service ratio of 11.7 percent, Thailand still qualifies as a "less indebted" country by World Bank standards.

But short-term debt's share of about 40-45 percent of the total outstanding in foreign currency debt was uncomfortable, economists said. Short-term debt is more costly when a country's currency is under pressure and interest rates rise.

While Thailand's economy boomed, portfolio investments which went mostly to the stock market also surged. Net portfolio investments leaped to $3.29 billion in 1995 from $1.11 billion in 1994, according to central bank data.
Final data for 1996 is not yet available, but analysts say the amount will have fallen after the Thai share market slumped in the second half of 1996.
In a bid to win the confidence of foreign investors, the Thai authorities last week decided to allow the baht to depreciate by nearly 20 percent in a managed float.

The surprise move triggered a strong rally in Thai stocks and raised hopes that the government will be able to trim interest rates to revive the economy, perhaps early in 1998. But analysts warn the quick turnaround in sentiment may not be sustainable now.
"I'm not too optimistic about things in Thailand yet," said Jimmy Koh, an economist at Singapore-based I.D.E.A.
He said he did not believe the baht's defacto devaluation would guarantee Thailand fund inflows because the ailing finance sector was still in focus.
Mergers ordered last month by the newly-appointed finance minister, Thanong Bidaya, have yet to take place.
Analysts say another factor hampering development of a government bond market was the strength of Thailand's commercial banks and the limited role of investment banks.

"The investment banks here are not strong enough to push for more debt issues. Commercial banks would naturally enjoy the spreads rather than the fees they would get from clients," a local investment bank executive said.
